introduction_markdown:
**Time allowed: three hours.** This paper contains six questions arranged in three sections: Section A - Physical and General Chemistry (questions 1 and 2); Section B - Inorganic Chemistry (questions 3 and 4); Section C - Organic Chemistry (questions 5 and 6).

Answer ALL the SIX questions in this booklet. The mark allocation is indicated for each question. Each question carries 20 marks. In calculations you are advised to show all the steps in your working, giving your answer at each stage. All necessary working must be shown. No marks will be awarded for answers without brief statements showing how the answers have been obtained. Noiseless calculators may be used.

**Useful data:** $R = 8.314\ \mathrm{J\,K^{-1}\,mol^{-1}}$ or $0.082\ \mathrm{atm\,dm^3\,K^{-1}\,mol^{-1}}$; one atmosphere (1 atm) = 1 Pa = $1.01\times10^{5}\ \mathrm{N\,m^{-2}}$ (as printed); relative atomic masses (RAM): C = 12.0, O = 16.0, S = 32.0, H = 1.0, Cl = 35.5.

questions.enonce_markdown:
Define the following:

(i) Mole of a substance.

(ii) Avogadro constant. *[2 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i)** A mole of a substance is the **amount of substance that contains as many elementary entities (atoms, molecules, ions, electrons...) as there are atoms in exactly 12 g of carbon-12**. One mole contains $6.02\times10^{23}$ entities.

**(ii)** The Avogadro constant, $L$ or $N_A$, is the **number of elementary entities per mole of substance**: $6.02\times10^{23}\ \mathrm{mol^{-1}}$ (the number of atoms in 12 g of carbon-12).

questions.enonce_markdown:
(i) 0.217 g of a volatile liquid produces 47.1 cm$^3$ of vapour at 60$^\circ$C and 2.16 atm. Calculate the molar mass of the liquid. ($R = 0.082\ \mathrm{atm\,dm^3\,K^{-1}\,mol^{-1}}$)

(ii) State the method used in the determination of the molar mass of a volatile liquid. *[3 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i)** Use the ideal gas equation $PV = nRT$ with $n = m/M$.

- $P = 2.16\ \mathrm{atm}$
- $V = 47.1\ \mathrm{cm^3} = 0.0471\ \mathrm{dm^3}$
- $T = 60 + 273 = 333\ \mathrm{K}$
- $R = 0.082\ \mathrm{atm\,dm^3\,K^{-1}\,mol^{-1}}$

$n = \dfrac{PV}{RT} = \dfrac{2.16 \times 0.0471}{0.082 \times 333} = \dfrac{0.1017}{27.31} = 3.73\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{mol}$

$M = \dfrac{m}{n} = \dfrac{0.217\ \mathrm{g}}{3.73\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{mol}} = 58.2\ \mathrm{g\,mol^{-1}}$

**Molar mass $\approx 58\ \mathrm{g\,mol^{-1}}$** (consistent with propanone, $\mathrm{C_3H_6O}$).

**(ii)** The **Victor Meyer method** (vapour density method): a known mass of the volatile liquid is vaporised in a heated tube; the vapour displaces an equal volume of air, which is collected over water and measured, together with the temperature and pressure. The volume of vapour of the known mass then gives the molar mass through $PV = nRT$. (A gas syringe method, in which the liquid is injected into a heated syringe, uses the same principle.)

questions.enonce_markdown:
Ionic bonds, covalent bonds and hydrogen bonds are all forces of attraction.

(i) Distinguish between an ionic bond and a covalent bond.

(ii) Give one condition necessary for the formation of hydrogen bonds. *[3 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i)**

| Ionic bond | Covalent bond |
|---|---|
| Electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions, formed by **transfer of electrons** from a metal atom to a non-metal atom | **Sharing of a pair of electrons** between two atoms (usually non-metals) |
| Non-directional; forms a giant ionic lattice (e.g. NaCl) | Directional; forms discrete molecules (e.g. $\mathrm{H_2O}$) or giant covalent structures |

**(ii)** A hydrogen bond forms when a **hydrogen atom is covalently bonded to a small, highly electronegative atom (F, O or N)** and is attracted to a **lone pair of electrons on another F, O or N atom** of a neighbouring molecule (for example $\mathrm{O{-}H \cdots O}$ in water and alcohols, or $\mathrm{N{-}H \cdots N}$ in ammonia).

questions.enonce_markdown:
Methane burns in a limited supply of oxygen to give carbon monoxide and water.

$\mathrm{CH_4(g)} + \tfrac{3}{2}\mathrm{O_2(g)} \longrightarrow \mathrm{CO(g)} + 2\mathrm{H_2O(g)}$

The standard enthalpy change of combustion of methane and carbon monoxide are $-890\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$ and $-283\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$ respectively.

(i) Sketch the energy cycle diagram that combines all the above combustion reactions.

(ii) Calculate the enthalpy change for the combustion of methane in limited supply of oxygen.

(iii) State Hess's Law. *[4 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i)** Energy cycle (Hess cycle): the reaction in limited oxygen (enthalpy change $\Delta H_x$) and the two complete combustions both end at the same products $\mathrm{CO_2} + 2\mathrm{H_2O}$.

```
 CH4(g) + 3/2 O2(g) ---------- dHx ----------> CO(g) + 2H2O
          \                                       /
           \  + 1/2 O2                           /  + 1/2 O2
            \  dHc(CH4) = -890 kJ/mol           /   dHc(CO) = -283 kJ/mol
             \                                 /
              v                               v
                      CO2(g) + 2H2O
```

(Route 1: $\mathrm{CH_4} + 2\mathrm{O_2} \rightarrow \mathrm{CO_2} + 2\mathrm{H_2O}$, $\Delta H = -890$ kJ. Route 2: $\mathrm{CH_4} + \tfrac32\mathrm{O_2} \rightarrow \mathrm{CO} + 2\mathrm{H_2O}$, $\Delta H_x$, then $\mathrm{CO} + \tfrac12\mathrm{O_2} \rightarrow \mathrm{CO_2}$, $\Delta H = -283$ kJ.)

**(ii)** By Hess's law, the two routes have the same total enthalpy change:

$\Delta H_x + (-283) = -890$

$\Delta H_x = -890 + 283 = \mathbf{-607\ kJ\,mol^{-1}}$

(The enthalpy change for the combustion of methane to carbon monoxide is $-607$ kJ per mole of methane.)

**(iii) Hess's law:** the total enthalpy change of a chemical reaction is **independent of the route taken** from reactants to products, provided the initial and final conditions are the same; it depends only on the initial and final states.

questions.enonce_markdown:
X-ray diffraction is one of the indirect methods used in determining the structure of crystals.

(i) What is x-ray diffraction?

(ii) In a potassium nitrite, $(\mathrm{KNO_2})$ crystal, x-rays of wavelength $1.55\times10^{-8}$ cm form a second-order cone at an angle of $8.92^\circ$. Calculate the spacing between the layers of ions in the crystal. *[3 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i)** X-ray diffraction is the **scattering of a beam of X-rays by the regularly arranged layers of atoms or ions in a crystal**. Because the wavelength of X-rays is of the same order as the spacing between the layers, the scattered rays interfere; reinforcement (constructive interference) occurs only at certain angles and gives a pattern of spots or rings on a photographic film or detector. The positions and intensities of the spots are used to calculate the distances between layers and so to deduce the arrangement of the particles in the crystal.

**(ii)** Use the **Bragg equation** $n\lambda = 2d\sin\theta$.

- $n = 2$ (second order)
- $\lambda = 1.55\times10^{-8}\ \mathrm{cm}$
- $\theta = 8.92^\circ$, $\sin 8.92^\circ = 0.1551$

$d = \dfrac{n\lambda}{2\sin\theta} = \dfrac{2 \times 1.55\times10^{-8}}{2 \times 0.1551} = 1.00\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{cm}$

**Spacing between the layers $d \approx 1.0\times10^{-7}$ cm** ($= 1.0\ \mathrm{nm}$).

questions.enonce_markdown:
A mixture comprising of 28 g of methanol and 36 g of ethanol obeys Raoult's law closely. At 30 $^\circ$C the vapour pressures of methanol and ethanol are 32 KPa and 20 KPa respectively. Calculate:

(i) Mole fraction of each component in the mixture.

(ii) Partial vapour pressure of each component in the mixture. *[4 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
Molar masses (RAM: C = 12.0, O = 16.0, H = 1.0): methanol $\mathrm{CH_3OH}$: $12 + 4 + 16 = 32\ \mathrm{g\,mol^{-1}}$; ethanol $\mathrm{C_2H_5OH}$: $24 + 6 + 16 = 46\ \mathrm{g\,mol^{-1}}$.

**(i) Mole fractions**

$n(\text{methanol}) = \dfrac{28}{32} = 0.875\ \mathrm{mol}$

$n(\text{ethanol}) = \dfrac{36}{46} = 0.783\ \mathrm{mol}$

$n_{\text{total}} = 0.875 + 0.783 = 1.658\ \mathrm{mol}$

$x(\text{methanol}) = \dfrac{0.875}{1.658} = 0.528$

$x(\text{ethanol}) = \dfrac{0.783}{1.658} = 0.472$ (the two add up to 1)

**(ii) Partial vapour pressures** (Raoult's law: $p_i = x_i\,p_i^\circ$)

$p(\text{methanol}) = 0.528 \times 32 = 16.9\ \mathrm{kPa}$

$p(\text{ethanol}) = 0.472 \times 20 = 9.44\ \mathrm{kPa}$

(Total vapour pressure of the mixture $= 16.9 + 9.44 = 26.3$ kPa.)
